column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 18: Fear Allah wherever you are

column2: Abū Dharr and Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“Fear Allah wherever you are; follow a bad deed with a good one and it will wipe it out; and treat people with good character.”
Al-Tirmidhī reported it and said: A ḥasan hadith; and in some copies: ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded this hadith by way of Sufyān al-Thawrī, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, from Maymūn ibn Abī Shabīb, from Abū Dharr.
He also recorded it with this chain from Maymūn, from Muʿādh, and he mentioned that his teacher Maḥmūd ibn Ghaylān said: The hadith of Abū Dharr is more authentic.

The chain of this hadith has been reported in different ways. It has also been given as mursal: from Ḥabīb, from Maymūn, that the Prophet ﷺ gave this advice; and al-Dāraquṭnī judged this mursal version the stronger.

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith ḥasan; the ṣaḥīḥ grading found in some copies is unlikely to be original. Al-Ḥākim, however, recorded it and said: Authentic according to the conditions of al-Bukhārī and Muslim. This is a mistake in two respects.

First, al-Bukhārī recorded nothing at all from Maymūn ibn Abī Shabīb — who is also called Ibn Shabīb — in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and Muslim recorded from him only a single hadith, from al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah, in the introduction to his book.

Second, it is not established that Maymūn ibn Abī Shabīb heard from any of the Companions. Al-Fallās said: In none of his narrations from the Companions does he say “I heard”, and I have not been told of anyone who claims that he heard from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ.
Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said: His narration from Abū Dharr and ʿĀʾishah is not connected.
Abū Dāwūd said: He did not live to meet ʿĀʾishah, and he did not see ʿAlī. That being so, still less did he meet Muʿādh.

The position of al-Bukhārī, of his teacher ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, of Abū Zurʿah, Abū Ḥātim and others is that a chain is not connected unless it is established that the narrators met. Imam Aḥmad's words point to this, and al-Shāfiʿī stated it explicitly in al-Risālah. All of this differs from the position of Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him).

It has been narrated by other routes that the Prophet ﷺ gave this advice to Muʿādh and to Abū Dharr. Al-Bazzār recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Lahīʿah, from Abū al-Zubayr, from Abū al-Ṭufayl, from Muʿādh,

that the Prophet ﷺ sent him to a people, and he said: O Messenger of Allah, advise me. He said: “Spread the greeting of peace, give food freely, and be shy before Allah as you would be shy before a man of standing in your family. When you do wrong, do good; and let your character be as good as you can make it.”
Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, that Muʿādh ibn Jabal was about to set out on a journey and said:
O Messenger of Allah, advise me. He said: “Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him.” He said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me more. He said: “When you do wrong, do good.” He said:
O Messenger of Allah, tell me more. He said: “Be upright, and let your character be good.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Darrāj, from Abū al-Haytham, from Abū Dharr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him:

“I counsel you to fear Allah in your affairs, secret and open. When you do wrong, do good. Never ask anyone for anything, even if your whip falls. Do not take charge of a trust, and do not judge between two people.”
He also recorded, from another hadith of Abū Dharr, that he said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, teach me a deed that will bring me near to Paradise and keep me far from the Fire.
He said: “When you do a bad deed, do a good deed, for it counts as ten like it.” I said: O Messenger of Allah, is “There is no god but Allah” one of the good deeds?
He said: “It is the best of good deeds.”
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr recorded in al-Tamhīd, with a chain that is open to question, that Anas said: The Prophet ﷺ sent Muʿādh to Yemen and said:

“Muʿādh, fear Allah, treat people with good character, and when you do a bad deed, follow it with a good one.” He said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, is “There is no god but Allah” one of the good deeds?
He said: “It is one of the greatest of good deeds.”
The Prophet's advice to Muʿādh ﷺ has also been narrated in a long version, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar and others, by routes that contain weakness.
The hadith of Abū Hurayrah also comes under this meaning: the Prophet ﷺ was asked what most often admits people into Paradise,
and he said: “Fear of Allah and good character.” Imam Aḥmad, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī recorded it, and al-Tirmidhī graded it authentic; Ibn Ḥibbān also recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

This is a great piece of advice that gathers together the rights of Allah and the rights of His servants. Allah's right over His servants is that they fear Him as He should be feared, and taqwā is Allah's counsel to the first and the last.
The Exalted said: “We have enjoined those who were given the Book before you, and you, to fear Allah” [al-Nisāʾ 4:131].

The root of taqwā is that the servant sets between himself and what he fears and dreads a shield (wiqāyah) that protects him from it. So the servant's taqwā of his Lord is that he sets between himself and what he dreads from his Lord — His anger, His displeasure and His punishment — a shield that protects him from it, which is to obey Him and avoid disobeying Him.
Sometimes taqwā is attached to the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as in the words of the Exalted, “Fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered” [al-Māʾidah 5:96], and His words:

“O you who believe, fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has sent ahead for tomorrow; and fear Allah, for Allah is aware of what you do” [al-Ḥashr 59:18]. When taqwā is attached to Him, Glorified and Exalted is He, the meaning is: beware of His displeasure and anger,

which is the greatest thing to be guarded against, and from which His punishment in this world and the Hereafter arises. The Exalted said, “Allah warns you of Himself” [Āl ʿImrān 3:28], and the Exalted said, “He is worthy to be feared, and worthy to forgive” [al-Muddaththir 74:56].

He, Glorified is He, is worthy to be feared, held in awe, revered and magnified in the hearts of His servants, so that they worship and obey Him, because of the reverence and honour He deserves and His attributes of grandeur and greatness, the might of His seizing and the severity of His force.

In al-Tirmidhī, Anas narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said about this verse, “He is worthy to be feared, and worthy to forgive”: “Allah the Exalted said: I am worthy to be feared; so whoever fears Me and does not set up another god with Me, I am worthy to forgive him.”

Sometimes taqwā is attached to Allah's punishment, and to its place, such as the Fire, or its time, such as the Day of Resurrection. The Exalted said: “Guard yourselves against the Fire, which has been prepared for the disbelievers” [Āl ʿImrān 3:131]; the Exalted said:

“Guard yourselves against the Fire whose fuel is people and stones, prepared for the disbelievers” [al-Baqarah 2:24]; the Exalted said: “Guard yourselves against a Day on which you will be returned to Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:281]; and the Exalted said: “Fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered” [al-Māʾidah 5:96], and “Guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another in the least” [al-Baqarah 2:48].

Complete taqwā includes doing obligations and leaving what is forbidden and what is doubtful; beyond that it may also include doing what is recommended and leaving what is disliked, which is the highest degree of taqwā. Allah the Exalted said:

“Alif Lām Mīm. That is the Book, in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing, who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided for them; and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and are certain of the Hereafter” [al-Baqarah 2:1–4].

And the Exalted said: “But righteousness is [that of] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets; who gives wealth, despite loving it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, those who ask, and for freeing slaves; who establishes the prayer and gives zakāh; those who fulfil their promises when they promise, and the patient in poverty, hardship and the time of battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is they who are the God-fearing” [al-Baqarah 2:177].
Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: On the Day of Resurrection a call will go out: Where are the God-fearing?
They will stand in the shelter of the Most Merciful, who will neither veil nor screen Himself from them. They asked him: Who are the God-fearing?
He said: People who guarded against shirk and the worship of idols, and were sincere to Allah in their worship.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: The God-fearing are those who beware of Allah's punishment for abandoning the guidance they know, and who hope for His mercy in believing what He has brought.
Al-Ḥasan said: The God-fearing guarded against what was forbidden to them and carried out what was made obligatory for them.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: Taqwā of Allah is not fasting by day and praying by night while mixing [good and bad] in between. Rather, taqwā of Allah is leaving what Allah has forbidden and carrying out what Allah has made obligatory; whoever is granted good beyond that, it is good upon good.

Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb said: Taqwā is that you act in obedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, hoping for Allah's reward; and that you leave disobedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, fearing Allah's punishment.

Abū al-Dardāʾ said: The completion of taqwā is that the servant fears Allah even in an atom's weight, so that he leaves some of what he sees as lawful for fear that it may be unlawful, as a barrier between himself and the unlawful.

For Allah has made clear to His servants what He will bring them to, saying: “Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it” [al-Zalzalah 99:7–8]. So never think any good too small to do, nor any evil too small to guard against.
Al-Ḥasan said: Taqwā stayed with the God-fearing until they left much that was lawful for fear of the unlawful.
Al-Thawrī said: They were called the God-fearing only
because they guarded against what is not normally guarded against.
Mūsā ibn Aʿyan said: The God-fearing kept themselves clear of some lawful things for fear of falling into the unlawful, and so Allah called them the God-fearing.
The hadith has already been cited: “The servant does not attain to being one of the God-fearing until he leaves what is harmless out of caution against what is harmful,”
and the hadith: “Whoever guards against doubtful matters has kept his religion and his honour clear.”
Maymūn ibn Mihrān said: The God-fearing person holds himself to account more strictly than a miserly partner holds his partner.

Ibn Masʿūd said about the words of the Exalted, “Fear Allah as He should be feared” [Āl ʿImrān 3:102]: That He be obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, and thanked and not met with ingratitude.
Al-Ḥākim recorded it as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ), but the mawqūf version, which stops short of him, is more authentic. Thanking Him includes doing every act of obedience.

The meaning of “remembered and not forgotten” is that the servant keeps Allah's commands in mind in his movement, his stillness and his words, and obeys them, and keeps His prohibitions in mind in all of that, and avoids them.
The word taqwā is often used chiefly for avoiding what is forbidden, as when Abū Hurayrah was asked about taqwā and said: Have you ever taken a road with thorns on it?
The man said: Yes. He said: What did you do?
He said: When I saw thorns, I stepped aside from them, stepped over them, or stopped short of them. He said: That is taqwā.
Ibn al-Muʿtazz took up this idea and said:
Leave sins, the small of them / and the great: that is piety.
Be like one who walks on ground / full of thorns, wary of what he sees.
Never think little of a small sin: / mountains are made of pebbles.

The root of taqwā is that the servant knows what is to be guarded against and then guards against it. ʿAwn ibn ʿAbdillāh said: The completion of taqwā is that you seek knowledge of what you do not yet know of it, in addition to what you do know.
Maʿrūf al-Karkhī related that Bakr ibn Khunays said: How can someone be God-fearing who does not know what to guard against?
Then Maʿrūf said: If you do not know well how to guard yourself, you will consume usury; if you do not know well how to guard yourself, a woman will meet you and you will not lower your gaze;
if you do not know well how to guard yourself, you will put your sword on your shoulder — and the Prophet ﷺ said to Muḥammad ibn Maslamah:
“When you see my community fall into dispute, take your sword and strike Uḥud with it.” Then Maʿrūf said: And this sitting of mine — perhaps we ought to have guarded against it.

Then he said: And your coming with me from the mosque to here — we ought to have guarded against it. Has it not come in the hadith, “It is a trial for the one followed and a humiliation for the follower”?
— meaning people walking behind a man.

In short, taqwā is Allah's counsel to all His creation and the counsel of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his community. When he ﷺ sent out a commander at the head of a raiding party, he would counsel him to fear Allah in his own conduct and to treat well the Muslims who were with him.
When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave his sermon on the Day of Sacrifice during the Farewell Pilgrimage, he counselled the people to fear Allah and to hear and obey their leaders.
When he admonished the people and they said to him, “It is as if this were the admonition of one bidding farewell, so counsel us,” he said:
“I counsel you to fear Allah, and to hear and obey.”
In the long hadith of Abū Dharr recorded by Ibn Ḥibbān and others: I said:
O Messenger of Allah, counsel me. He said: “I counsel you to fear Allah, for it is the head of the whole affair.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, that he said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, counsel me. He said: “I counsel you to fear Allah, for it is the head of everything; and hold to jihād, for it is the monasticism of Islam.”
Others recorded it with the wording: “Hold to the fear of Allah, for it gathers all good.”

In al-Tirmidhī, Yazīd ibn Salamah asked the Prophet ﷺ: O Messenger of Allah, I have heard many hadiths from you, and I fear that the last of them will make me forget the first; so tell me a word that will be comprehensive. He said: “Fear Allah in what you know.”

The righteous Salaf never stopped counselling one another with it. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say in his sermons: To proceed: I counsel you to fear Allah, to praise Him as He deserves,

to mix hope with dread, and to join earnest pleading to your asking. For Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, praised Zakariyyā and his household, saying: “They used to hasten to good deeds and call on Us in hope and dread, and they were humble before Us” [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:90].
When death came to him and he appointed ʿUmar as his successor, he called him and gave him his counsel, and the first thing he said to him was: Fear Allah, ʿUmar.

ʿUmar wrote to his son ʿAbdullāh: To proceed: I counsel you to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for whoever fears Him, He protects; whoever lends to Him, He repays; and whoever thanks Him, He gives more. So keep taqwā before your eyes and let it be the polish of your heart.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib appointed a man over a raiding party and said to him: I counsel you to fear Allah, whom you must certainly meet, short of whom there is no end for you, and who owns this world and the Hereafter.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to a man: I counsel you to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic — the taqwā without which He accepts nothing, to whose people alone He shows mercy, and for which alone He rewards. Those who preach it are many, and those who practise it are few. May Allah make us and you among the God-fearing.

When he took office, he gave a sermon. He praised and extolled Allah, and said: I counsel you to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for fear of Allah can replace everything, but nothing can replace fear of Allah.
A man said to Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd: Counsel me. He said: I counsel you to fear Allah and to do good, for “Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good” [al-Naḥl 16:128].
A man who was setting out for Ḥajj said to him: Counsel me. He said to him: Fear Allah, for whoever fears Allah need feel no loneliness.
One of the Successors was asked at his death: Counsel us. He said: I counsel you with the end of Sūrat al-Naḥl: “Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good” [al-Naḥl 16:128].

One of the Salaf wrote to a brother of his: I counsel you to fear Allah, for it is the noblest thing you can keep in secret, the finest thing you can show openly and the best thing you can store up. May Allah help us and you to it, and secure its reward for us and for you.

Another of them wrote to a brother of his: I counsel you, and ourselves, to have taqwā, for it is the best provision for the Hereafter and for this life. Make it your path to every good and your refuge from every evil, for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has guaranteed its people deliverance from what they dread and provision from where they do not expect.

Shuʿbah said: Whenever I wanted to set out on a journey, I would say to al-Ḥakam: Do you need anything? He would say: I counsel you with what the Prophet ﷺ counselled Muʿādh ibn Jabal: “Fear Allah wherever you are; follow a bad deed with a good one and it will wipe it out; and treat people with good character.”
It is firmly established that the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: “O Allah, I ask You for guidance, taqwā, chastity and sufficiency.”

Abū Dharr said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse, “Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him” [al-Ṭalāq 65:2], and then said: “Abū Dharr, if all people held to it, it would suffice them.”
His words ﷺ, “Fear Allah wherever you are”, mean in private and in public, where people see him and where they do not. We have cited from the hadith of Abū Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ said to him:

“I counsel you to fear Allah in your affairs, secret and open.” The Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: “I ask You for fear of You in the unseen and the seen.” Fear of Allah in the unseen and the seen is one of the things that bring salvation.
We have already cited, from the hadith of Abū al-Ṭufayl, from Muʿādh, that the Prophet ﷺ said to him:
“Be shy before Allah as you would be shy before a man of standing in your family.” This is the cause that produces fear of Allah in private. For whoever knows that Allah sees him wherever he is,

and that He sees his inner and outer self, his secret and his open life, and keeps this in mind when he is alone, will be led by it to leave sins in private. The Qurʾān points to this meaning in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: “Fear Allah, by whom you ask one another, and [respect] the ties of the womb. Indeed, Allah is ever watchful over you” [al-Nisāʾ 4:1].

One of the Salaf used to say to his companions: May Allah give us and you the renunciation of the unlawful shown by someone who has the chance of it in private, knows that Allah sees him, and leaves it out of fear of Him — or words to that effect.
Al-Shāfiʿī said: The rarest things are three: generosity when one has little, scrupulousness in private, and a word of truth before someone from whom one hopes for something or whom one fears.

Ibn al-Sammāk the preacher wrote to a brother of his: To proceed: I counsel you to fear Allah, who is your intimate confidant in your secret life and your watcher in your open life. So keep Allah in your mind in every state, by night and by day,

and fear Allah in proportion to His nearness to you and His power over you. Know that you are under His eye: you will not leave His authority for anyone else's, nor His dominion for anyone else's. So let your wariness of Him be great and your dread of Him abundant. Peace.
Abū al-Jald said: Allah the Exalted revealed to one of the prophets: Say to your people: Why do you hide your sins from My creatures and show them to Me?
If you think I do not see you, you are associating partners with Me; and if you think that I see you, why have you made Me the least regarded of those who look at you?

Wuhayb ibn al-Ward used to say: Fear Allah in proportion to His power over you, and be shy before Him in proportion to His nearness to you. A man said to him: Admonish me. He said: Fear Allah, lest He be the least regarded of those who look at you.
One of the Salaf used to say: Do you suppose you would show mercy to someone who did not dare commit an offence against you until he knew that no eye but yours could see him?

Another of them said: Son of Ādam, if, while some eye was watching you, the way was not clear for your sin, and then, when you were alone with Allah only, the way was clear for you to disobey Him, and you felt less shy before Him than before some of His creatures,

you are one of two men: if you thought He does not see you, you have disbelieved; and if you knew He sees you and yet what restrained you before the weakest of His creatures did not restrain you before Him, you have been very bold towards Him.
A man went into a thicket of trees and said: If I were alone here with a sin, who would see me?
Then he heard a voice that filled the thicket: “Does He who created not know, when He is the Subtle, the All-Aware?” [al-Mulk 67:14].
A man tried to seduce a Bedouin woman, and said to her: No one sees us but the stars. She said: Then where is the One who made them stars?
Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir saw a man standing and talking with a woman, and said: Allah sees you both. May Allah screen us and you.
Al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī said: Watchfulness (murāqabah) is the heart's knowledge of the Lord's nearness.
Al-Junayd was asked what helps one to lower one's gaze, and he said: Your knowing that Allah's gaze upon you comes before your gaze upon what you look at.
Imam Aḥmad used to recite:
If you are ever alone one day, do not say, / “I am alone”; say rather, “There is a watcher over me.”
Do not think that Allah is heedless for a moment, / or that what is hidden is concealed from Him.
Ibn al-Sammāk used to recite:
You who persist in sin, are you not ashamed, / when Allah is the second with you when you are alone?
You have been deluded by your Lord's giving you respite / and His long covering of your wrongs.

The point is that when the Prophet ﷺ counselled Muʿādh to fear Allah in private and in public, he guided him to what would help him in that: to be shy before Allah as he would be shy before a man of standing among his people.
This means that he should constantly feel in his heart Allah's nearness to him and His seeing him, and so feel shy of His gaze upon him.

Muʿādh carried out what the Prophet ﷺ counselled him. ʿUmar had sent him to take charge of a post, and he came back with nothing. His wife reproached him, and he said: There was someone with me keeping a tight hold on me —

meaning someone who constrained him and prevented him from taking anything; by this Muʿādh meant his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. His wife thought that ʿUmar had sent an overseer with him, and she went about complaining of ʿUmar to people.

Whoever attains this station as a constant or prevailing state is one of those who act with excellence (muḥsinūn), who worship Allah as though they see Him, and one of those who act with excellence “who avoid the major sins and indecencies, except for lesser faults” [al-Najm 53:32].
In short, fearing Allah in private is the sign of complete faith, and it does much to make Allah place praise of the one who has it in the hearts of the believers.

In the hadith: “No servant keeps a secret but Allah clothes him in its cloak openly: if it is good, then good, and if it is evil, then evil.” This has been narrated as marfūʿ, and it has also been narrated as the words of Ibn Masʿūd.

Abū al-Dardāʾ said: Let each of you beware lest the hearts of the believers curse him without his realising it. He commits acts of disobedience to Allah when alone, and Allah casts hatred of him into the hearts of the believers.
Sulaymān al-Taymī said: A man may commit a sin in secret and wake up in the morning with its disgrace upon him. Someone else said: A servant may commit a sin between himself and Allah,

then come to his brothers, and they see its trace on him. This is one of the greatest proofs of the existence of the true God, who requites the smallest particles of deeds in this world before the Hereafter,
with whom no worker's deed is lost, and against whose power no veil or covering is of any use. So the happy one is he who sets right what is between himself and Allah,

for whoever sets right what is between himself and Allah, Allah sets right what is between him and people; and whoever seeks people's praise at the cost of Allah's displeasure, those people who praised him turn to blaming him.
Abū Sulaymān said: The loser is he who shows people his good deeds and openly flaunts what is ugly before Him who is nearer to him than his jugular vein.
One of the most remarkable things narrated on this is what is narrated from Abū Jaʿfar al-Sāʾiḥ, who said: Ḥabīb Abū Muḥammad was a merchant who lent money at interest. One day he passed by

some boys who were playing, and one said to another: Here comes the eater of usury! He hung his head and said: My Lord, You have disclosed my secret to the boys. He went back and gathered all his wealth, and said:

My Lord, I am a captive, and I have bought myself from You with this wealth, so set me free. In the morning he gave all the wealth away in charity and devoted himself to worship. Then one day he passed by those same boys,
and when they saw him, one said to another: Be quiet, here comes Ḥabīb the worshipper! He wept and said: My Lord, You blame at one time and praise at another, and all of it is from You.

As for his words ﷺ, “Follow a bad deed with a good one and it will wipe it out”: since the servant is commanded to have taqwā in private and in public, and yet some shortfall in taqwā must inevitably come from him at times, whether by neglecting some of what is commanded

or by committing some of what is forbidden, he commanded him to do what would wipe out this bad deed, namely to follow it with a good one. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember” [Hūd 11:114].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Ibn Masʿūd narrated that a man kissed a woman and then came to the Prophet ﷺ
and told him of it. The Prophet ﷺ remained silent until this verse was revealed; then he called him and recited it to him. A man said: Is this for him in particular?
He said: “No, it is for people generally.”
Allah has described the God-fearing in His Book in terms like those of the Prophet's counsel ﷺ here, in the words of the Mighty and Majestic:

“Hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and to a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing, who spend in ease and in hardship, who restrain their rage and pardon people — and Allah loves those who do good — and who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins but Allah? — and do not persist knowingly in what they have done. Their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding in them for ever. How excellent is the reward of those who work!” [Āl ʿImrān 3:133–136].

He described the God-fearing as dealing with people by doing good to them through spending, restraining their rage and pardoning them, so combining in their description open-handed giving and the bearing of harm. This is the utmost of the good character that the Prophet ﷺ counselled Muʿādh to have. Then He described them as those who,

“when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins”, and do not persist in them. This shows that the God-fearing may sometimes commit major sins, which are the indecencies,

and minor sins, which are wronging oneself, but they do not persist in them; rather, they remember Allah as soon as they commit them, ask His forgiveness and repent to Him of them. Repentance is giving up persistence in sin.
The meaning of His words “remember Allah” is that they remember His greatness, the severity of His seizing and His vengeance, and the punishment He has threatened for disobedience,

and this leads them to return at once, ask forgiveness and give up persisting. Allah the Exalted said: “Those who fear Allah, when a passing thought from Satan touches them, remember, and at once they see clearly” [al-Aʿrāf 7:201].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A servant committed a sin and said: My Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me. Allah said: My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sin

and takes to account for sin; I have forgiven My servant. Then he committed another sin…” — until he said, the fourth time — “so let him do what he wishes,” meaning: as long as he remains in this state, asking forgiveness every time he sins.

In al-Tirmidhī, from the hadith of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever asks forgiveness has not persisted, even if he goes back to it seventy times a day.”
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said:
O Messenger of Allah, one of us commits a sin. He said: “It is recorded against him.” He said: Then he asks forgiveness for it. He said: “He is forgiven, and his repentance is accepted.” He said:

Then he goes back and sins again. He said: “It is recorded against him.” He said: Then he asks forgiveness for it and repents. He said: “He is forgiven, and his repentance is accepted; and Allah does not grow weary until you grow weary.”

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded with a weak chain that ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: Ḥabīb ibn al-Ḥārith came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, I am a man much given to sins. He said:

“Then repent to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” He said: I repent, then I go back to it. He said: “Then every time you sin, repent.” He said: O Messenger of Allah, then my sins will be many. He said: “Allah's pardon is more than your sins, Ḥabīb ibn al-Ḥārith.”
Al-Ṭabarānī also recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Anas as marfūʿ, with a weak chain.

And with his chain, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: Whoever remembers a wrong he has done, and his heart trembles at it, and he asks Allah's forgiveness, nothing holds it back until it is wiped out.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated, with his chain of narration, that ʿAlī said: The best of you are all those who are often tried and often repent. He was asked: And if he goes back to it?
He said: He asks Allah's forgiveness and repents. He was asked: And if he goes back to it?
He said: He asks Allah's forgiveness and repents. He was asked: And if he goes back to it?
He said: He asks Allah's forgiveness and repents. He was asked: For how long?
He said: Until it is Satan who is worn out.
Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd as marfūʿ: “One who repents of a sin is like one who has no sin.”

Al-Ḥasan was asked: Should one of us not be ashamed before his Lord, asking forgiveness for his sins and then going back to them, then asking forgiveness and going back again? He said: Satan would love to gain this from you; so do not grow weary of asking forgiveness.

It is narrated that he said: I see this only as one of the traits of the believers — meaning that every time the believer sins, he repents. It has been narrated: “The believer is often tried and often repents.”
It has been narrated as marfūʿ, from the hadith of Jābir with a weak chain: “The believer is frayed and patching; happy is he who dies while patching.”

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said in his sermon: Whoever among you does well, let him praise Allah; and whoever does wrong, let him ask Allah's forgiveness and repent. For people cannot avoid doing deeds that Allah has hung around their necks and written for them.

In another narration from him, he said: O people, whoever falls into a sin, let him ask Allah's forgiveness and repent; if he goes back to it, let him ask Allah's forgiveness and repent; and if he goes back to it, let him ask Allah's forgiveness and repent. They are only wrongs hung around men's necks, and destruction, utter destruction, lies in persisting in them.

The meaning of this is that the servant cannot avoid doing the sins decreed for him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: “The son of Ādam's share of fornication has been written for him, and he will come to it without fail.”

But Allah has given the servant a way out of the sins he falls into, through repentance and asking forgiveness. If he does that, he is freed from the evil of the sin; and if he persists in the sin, he is destroyed.
In the Musnad, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Show mercy and you will be shown mercy; forgive and you will be forgiven. Woe to the funnels of speech; woe to those who persist, who persist knowingly in what they have done.” The funnels of speech were explained as those whose ears are like funnels for the wisdom and good admonition they hear:
when any of it enters one ear, it goes out of the other, and they gain no benefit from anything they hear.
The good deed in his words ﷺ, “Follow a bad deed with a good one”, may mean repentance from that bad deed.
This is stated explicitly in a mursal hadith that Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded among the mursal reports of Muḥammad ibn Jubayr: when the Prophet ﷺ sent Muʿādh to Yemen, he said:

“Muʿādh, fear Allah as much as you can; act for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with your strength as far as you are able; remember Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, at every tree and stone; and if you commit a sin, make a fresh repentance for it — if in secret, then in secret, and if in public, then in public.”
Abū Nuʿaym recorded something with the same meaning by another, weak route from Muʿādh.
Qatādah said: Salmān said: If you do a bad deed in secret, do a good deed in secret; and if you do a bad deed in public, do a good deed in public, so that the one may answer for the other.
He may have meant repentance by the good deed, or something more general.
Allah has told us in many places in His Book that whoever repents of his sin is forgiven his sin, or has his repentance accepted, as in the words of the Exalted:

“Repentance accepted by Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after; it is they whose repentance Allah accepts” [al-Nisāʾ 4:17]; His words: “Then your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance and then repented after that and set things right — after that your Lord is Forgiving, Merciful” [al-Naḥl 16:119];

His words: “Except for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds: for them Allah will change their bad deeds into good deeds” [al-Furqān 25:70]; His words: “I am Most Forgiving towards whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, and then follows guidance” [Ṭā Hā 20:82]; His words:

“Except for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds: they will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least” [Maryam 19:60]; and His words: “And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins but Allah?” [Āl ʿImrān 3:135] — the two verses.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān informed us, from Thābit, from Anas, who said: I have been told that when this verse was revealed — “And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins” — Iblīs wept.
It is narrated that Ibn Masʿūd said: This verse is better for sinners than this world and all that is in it.
Ibn Sīrīn said: Allah has given us this verse in place of what He prescribed for the Children of Israel as expiations for their sins.
Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī said, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: A man said: O Messenger of Allah, if only our expiations were like the expiations of the Children of Israel!
The Prophet ﷺ said: “O Allah, we do not want them” — three times — “what Allah has given you is better than what He gave the Children of Israel.

When one of the Children of Israel committed a wrong, he would find it written on his door together with its expiation. If he made the expiation, it was a disgrace in this world; and if he did not, it was a disgrace for him in the Hereafter.

What Allah has given you is better than what He gave the Children of Israel. He said: ‘Whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then asks Allah's forgiveness, will find Allah Forgiving, Merciful’” [al-Nisāʾ 4:110].

Ibn ʿAbbās said about the words of the Exalted, “He has not placed any hardship upon you in religion” [al-Ḥajj 22:78]: This is the breadth of Islam, and the repentance and expiation that Allah has given the community of Muḥammad.

The apparent sense of these texts is that whoever repents to Allah with sincere repentance, and in whose case the conditions of repentance are all met, can be certain that Allah accepts his repentance,

just as one can be certain that a disbeliever's Islam is accepted when he accepts Islam sincerely. This is the view of the majority, and the words of Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr indicate that there is consensus on it.
Some people said: One cannot be certain that repentance is accepted; it is only hoped for, and the one who repents is still subject to the divine will. They cited His words:

“Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills” [al-Nisāʾ 4:48], for He placed all sins under His will. They may also cite words of the Exalted such as:

“O you who believe, repent to Allah with sincere repentance; it may be that your Lord will remove your bad deeds from you” [al-Taḥrīm 66:8], His words: “As for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, it may be that he will be among the successful” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:67],

His words: “Repent to Allah all together, O believers, that you may succeed” [al-Nūr 24:31], and His words: “Others have acknowledged their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. It may be that Allah will turn to them in mercy” [al-Tawbah 9:102].
The apparent sense is that this [last verse] concerns those who repent,

because acknowledgement implies remorse, and in the hadith of ʿĀʾishah the Prophet ﷺ said: “When the servant acknowledges his sin and then repents, Allah accepts his repentance.” The correct view is that of the majority.

These verses do not show that there is no certainty, for when the Generous raises a hope, He does not cut off the hope He has raised. That is why Ibn ʿAbbās said: “It may be” (ʿasā), from Allah, is binding. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah transmitted this from him.
The reward of faith and righteous deeds has also come with the words “it may be”, and that does not show that it is uncertain, as in His words:

“The mosques of Allah are maintained only by whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, establishes the prayer, gives zakāh and fears none but Allah. It may be that those will be among the rightly guided” [al-Tawbah 9:18].
As for His words, “He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills”, the one who repents is among those He wills to forgive, as He has told us in many places in His Book.
The good deed in the Prophet's words ﷺ, “Follow a bad deed with a good one”, may also mean something more general than repentance, as in the words of the Exalted:

“Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds” [Hūd 11:114]. It has been narrated, from the hadith of Muʿādh, that the Prophet ﷺ commanded the man on whose account this verse was revealed to perform wuḍūʾ and pray.

Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no man who commits a sin,

then gets up, purifies himself, prays and asks Allah's forgiveness, but Allah forgives him.” Then he recited this verse: “And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins” [Āl ʿImrān 3:135].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs: ʿUthmān performed wuḍūʾ, then said: I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ perform wuḍūʾ like this wuḍūʾ of mine, and then he said:
“Whoever performs wuḍūʾ like this wuḍūʾ of mine and then prays two rakʿahs in which he does not let his mind wander, his past sins are forgiven.”

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, Abū al-Dardāʾ said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whoever performs wuḍūʾ and does it well, then stands and prays two or four rakʿahs, performing their bowing and humility well, and then asks Allah's forgiveness, is forgiven.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Anas said: I was with the Prophet ﷺ when a man came and said: O Messenger of Allah, I have committed an offence carrying a prescribed punishment, so carry it out on me. He did not ask him about it.

The time for prayer came and he prayed with the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet ﷺ had finished the prayer, the man stood up and went to him and said: O Messenger of Allah, I have committed an offence carrying a prescribed punishment, so apply the Book of Allah to me. He said: “Did you not pray with us?”
He said: Yes. He said: “Then Allah has forgiven you your sin” — or he said: “your offence.”
Muslim recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, and Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī recorded it by another route from Abū Umāmah, in whose hadith he said:

“You are as free of your wrong as on the day your mother bore you, so do not do it again.” And Allah revealed: “Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds” [Hūd 11:114].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Tell me, if there were a river at the door of one of you in which he bathed five times every day, would any of his dirt remain?”
They said: None of his dirt would remain. He said: “That is the likeness of the five prayers: by them Allah wipes out wrongs.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿUthmān narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever performs wuḍūʾ and does it well, his wrongs leave his body, even from beneath his nails.”
Also in it, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Shall I not direct you to that by which Allah wipes out wrongs and raises degrees?”

They said: Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah. He said: “Performing wuḍūʾ thoroughly in difficult conditions, taking many steps to the mosques, and waiting for one prayer after another. That is the guarding of the frontier (ribāṭ); that is the guarding of the frontier.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever fasts Ramaḍān out of faith and seeking its reward, his past sins are forgiven;

whoever stands in prayer in Ramaḍān out of faith and seeking its reward, his past sins are forgiven; and whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree out of faith and seeking its reward, his past sins are forgiven.”
Also in both, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever performs Ḥajj to this House without obscenity or wickedness comes out of his sins as on the day his mother bore him.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Islam wipes out what came before it, emigration wipes out what came before it, and Ḥajj wipes out what came before it.”
Also in it, from the hadith of Abū Qatādah, the Prophet ﷺ said about the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ:
“I hope from Allah that it will expiate the year before it”; and he said about the fast of the Day of ʿArafah:
“I hope from Allah that it will expiate the year before it and the year after it.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The likeness of one who does bad deeds and then does good deeds

is that of a man wearing a tight coat of mail that is choking him. Then he does a good deed, and one ring comes loose; then he does another good deed, and another comes loose, until it falls to the ground.”

Among the things that expiate wrongs is the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We mentioned earlier that the Prophet ﷺ was asked whether saying “There is no god but Allah” is one of the good deeds,
and he said: “It is the best of good deeds.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says ‘Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him’ a hundred times in a day, his wrongs are removed, even if they are like the foam of the sea.”

Also in both, from him, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says, ‘There is no god but Allah alone, without partner; His is the dominion and His is the praise; He gives life and causes death, and He has power over all things,’ a hundred times in a day,

it is equal for him to freeing ten slaves, a hundred good deeds are written for him, a hundred bad deeds are wiped out from him, and it is a protection for him from Satan that day until evening; and no one brings anything better than what he has brought, except someone who has done more than that.”
In the Musnad and the book of Ibn Mājah, Umm Hāniʾ narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“‘There is no god but Allah’ leaves no sin, and no deed surpasses it.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ passed by a tree with dry leaves and struck it with his stick, and the leaves fell in a shower. He said:
“‘Praise be to Allah’, ‘Glory be to Allah’, ‘There is no god but Allah’ and ‘Allah is greatest’ make the servant's sins fall away as the leaves of this tree fall.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded with an authentic chain from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “‘Glory be to Allah’, ‘Praise be to Allah’, ‘There is no god but Allah’ and ‘Allah is greatest’ shake off wrongs as a tree sheds its leaves.”
There are a great many hadiths on this; citing them would make the book long.
Al-Ḥasan was asked about a man who does not shrink from any sin, except that his tongue never tires of the remembrance of Allah. He said: That is a good help.
Imam Aḥmad was asked about a man who earned wealth from a doubtful source: do his prayer and glorification of Allah remove any of that from him?
He said: If he prays and glorifies Allah intending that, I hope so. Allah the Exalted said:
“They mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. It may be that Allah will turn to them in mercy” [al-Tawbah 9:102].
Mālik ibn Dīnār said: Weeping over a wrong removes wrongs as the wind strips dry leaves.
ʿAṭāʾ said: Whoever sits in one gathering of remembrance expiates by it ten gatherings of falsehood.

Shuways al-ʿAdawī — who was one of the early Successors — said: The companion on the right is commander — or he said: trustee — over the companion on the left. When the son of Ādam does a bad deed and the companion on the left wants to record it,

the companion on the right says to him: Do not be hasty; perhaps he will do a good deed. If he does a good deed, he cancels one [bad deed] with one [good deed], and nine good deeds are recorded for him. Then Satan says: Woe to him! Who can keep up with the multiplying of the son of Ādam's deeds?

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a chain open to question, from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When the son of Ādam sleeps, the angel says to the devil: Give me your scroll. He gives it to him, and for every good deed he finds in his own scroll,

he wipes out ten bad deeds from the devil's scroll and writes them as good deeds. So when one of you wants to sleep, let him say ‘Allah is greatest’ thirty-three times, ‘Praise be to Allah’ thirty-four times and ‘Glory be to Allah’ thirty-three times: that makes a hundred.” This is a gharīb and munkar hadith.

Wakīʿ narrated: al-Aʿmash told us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, who said: ʿAbdullāh — meaning Ibn Masʿūd — said: I would love to be granted terms by which every day I do nine wrongs and one good deed.
By this he indicates that the one good deed wipes out the nine wrongs and that one multiple of the good deed's reward is left over for him, and he would be content with that. And Allah knows best.
People have differed over two questions.
The first: do righteous deeds expiate both major and minor sins, or do they expiate only the minor ones?
Some said they expiate only minor sins. This has been narrated from ʿAṭāʾ and others of the Salaf concerning wuḍūʾ: that it expiates minor sins.
Salmān al-Fārisī said about wuḍūʾ: It expiates small wounds; walking to the mosque expiates more than that; and the prayer expiates more than that.
Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī recorded it.
As for major sins, they require repentance,

because Allah commanded His servants to repent and declared whoever does not repent a wrongdoer, and the community is agreed that repentance is obligatory; and obligations are fulfilled only with intention and purpose.
If major sins were expiated by wuḍūʾ, prayer and performing the other pillars of Islam, there would be no need for repentance, and that is false by consensus.

Moreover, if major sins were expiated by doing the obligations, no one who performed the obligations would be left with any sin for which to enter the Fire. That resembles the view of the Murjiʾah, and it is false.
This is what Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned in his book al-Tamhīd. He reported the consensus of the Muslims on it and cited hadiths as evidence.
Among them are the words of the Prophet ﷺ: “The five prayers, from one Friday to the next,

and from one Ramaḍān to the next, are expiations for what is between them, as long as major sins are avoided.” It is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, and it shows that these obligations do not expiate major sins.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reported in his Tafsīr two views on the meaning of this hadith. The first — which he reported from the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah — is that avoiding major sins is a condition for these obligations to expiate minor sins; if major sins are not avoided, these obligations expiate nothing at all.

The second is that they expiate minor sins unconditionally, though they do not expiate major sins, even if these are present — but on condition of repenting of the minor sins and not persisting in them. He preferred this view and reported it from the most discerning scholars.
By “on condition of repenting of the minor sins and not persisting in them” he means that if one persists in them they become major, and so deeds do not expiate them.
The first view he reported is unusual, though the like of it has also been reported from Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Jaʿfar among the scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿUthmān narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“There is no Muslim at the time of an obligatory prayer who performs its wuḍūʾ, its humility and its bowing well, but it is an expiation for the sins before it, as long as he does not commit a major sin; and that is for all time.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, Salmān narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “A man does not purify himself” — meaning on Friday — “doing it well,

then come to the Friday prayer and listen in silence until the imam finishes his prayer, but it is an expiation for what is between it and the next Friday, as long as the deadly major sins are avoided.”
Al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, there is no servant who prays the five prayers, fasts Ramaḍān, pays the zakāh and avoids the seven major sins, but the gates of Paradise are opened for him and he is told: Enter in peace.”
Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī also recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Abū Ayyūb, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Ḥākim recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ.

It is narrated as marfūʿ from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: Son of Ādam, remember Me for an hour at the beginning of the day and an hour at the end of the day, and I will forgive you what is between them — except the major sins, unless you repent of them.”
Ibn Masʿūd said: The five prayers are expiations for what is between them, as long as major sins are avoided.
Salmān said: Guard these five prayers, for they are expiations for these wounds as long as you do not suffer the deadly one.
Ibn ʿUmar said to a man: Do you fear entering the Fire, and would you love to enter Paradise?
He said: Yes. He said: Be dutiful to your mother. By Allah, if you speak gently to her and feed her, you will surely enter Paradise, as long as you avoid the sins that make the Fire due.
Qatādah said: Allah has promised forgiveness only to those who avoid major sins. We have been told that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Avoid the major sins, keep to what is right, and rejoice.”

A group of the hadith scholars and others held that these deeds expiate major sins; among them was Ibn Ḥazm al-Ẓāhirī, and it was he whom Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr had in mind in al-Tamhīd when he refuted this view. He said:

I would have preferred not to speak on this subject at all, were it not for the words of that speaker. I feared that some ignorant person might be deceived by them and plunge into the deadly sins, relying on their being expiated by the prayers, without remorse, asking forgiveness or repentance. It is Allah we ask for protection and success.

I say: Something like this occurs in the words of a group of hadith scholars about wuḍūʾ and the like, and something like it occurs in the words of Ibn al-Mundhir about standing in prayer on the Night of Decree. He said: It is hoped that whoever stands in prayer on it will be forgiven all his sins, small and great.
If what they mean is that whoever performs the obligations of Islam while persisting in major sins is certainly forgiven those major sins, this is certainly false;

its falsehood is known as a matter of necessity in the religion. We have already cited the words of the Prophet ﷺ: “Whoever does evil in Islam is taken to account for the first and the last” — meaning
for his deeds in the Jāhiliyyah and in Islam. This is too obvious to need explaining. But if this speaker means that whoever gives up persisting in major sins
and keeps up the obligations, without repentance or remorse for what he did before, has all his sins expiated by that — citing the apparent sense of His words:
“If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove your bad deeds from you and admit you by a noble entrance” [al-Nisāʾ 4:31].

He would say: “Bad deeds” covers major and minor sins alike; so just as minor sins are expiated by avoiding major ones, without purpose or intention, so too are major sins. One might also argue for this that Allah has promised the believers and the God-fearing forgiveness and the removal of bad deeds,

as is mentioned in more than one place in the Qurʾān, and this man has become one of the God-fearing, since he has done the obligations and avoided the major sins, and avoiding major sins needs no intention or purpose — if that is what is meant, this view can be maintained in general terms.
The correct view is that of the majority: major sins are not expiated without repentance,
because repentance is obligatory on the servants, and the Mighty and Majestic has said: “Whoever does not repent — it is they who are the wrongdoers” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:11].

The Companions, such as ʿUmar, ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, explained repentance as remorse, and some of them explained it as resolving not to return to the sin. This has been narrated as marfūʿ by a route containing weakness,
but no one among the Companions is known to have disagreed on this, nor among the Successors and those after them, such as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥasan and others.

As for the many texts that speak of the forgiveness of sins and the removal of bad deeds for the God-fearing, such as the words of the Exalted, “If you fear Allah, He will give you a criterion, remove your bad deeds from you and forgive you” [al-Anfāl 8:29], and the words of the Exalted, “Whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, He will remove his bad deeds from him and admit him to Gardens beneath which rivers flow” [al-Taghābun 64:9],

and His words, “Whoever fears Allah, He will remove his bad deeds from him and make his reward great” [al-Ṭalāq 65:5] — these verses do not spell out the traits of taqwā or what righteous deeds are, and among these is sincere repentance; whoever does not repent is a wrongdoer and not God-fearing.

In Sūrat Āl ʿImrān He has set out the traits of taqwā whose people He forgives and admits to Paradise, and among them He mentioned asking forgiveness and not persisting. So He guaranteed the removal of bad deeds and the forgiveness of sins only to those who answer this description. And Allah knows best.
Among the evidence that major sins are not expiated without repentance from them or punishment for them is the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, who said:

We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: “Pledge allegiance to me that you will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit fornication” — and he recited the verse to them — “Whoever of you fulfils this,

his reward rests with Allah. Whoever commits any of these and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him. And whoever commits any of these and Allah conceals it for him, his affair rests with Allah:

if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him.” It is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. In a narration of Muslim's: “Whoever of you commits an offence carrying a prescribed punishment and it is carried out on him, that is his expiation.”
This shows that the prescribed punishments are expiations.
Al-Shāfiʿī said: I have heard nothing on this subject — that the prescribed punishment is an expiation for those who receive it — better than the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit.

His words, “and is punished for it”, cover the punishments of the Sharīʿah, whether prescribed punishments with a fixed measure or those without one, such as discretionary punishments; and they include the punishments of divine decree, such as calamities, illnesses and pains.
For it is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: “No fatigue, illness, worry or grief befalls a Muslim — even a thorn that pricks him — but Allah expiates some of his wrongs by it.”

It has been narrated from ʿAlī that the prescribed punishment is an expiation for the one on whom it is carried out. Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī mentioned disagreement on this question and preferred the view that carrying out the punishment is in itself an expiation, and he strongly discounted the contrary view.

I say: It has been narrated from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym that carrying out the punishment is not an expiation and must be accompanied by repentance. A group of later scholars preferred this,

among them al-Baghawī and Abū ʿAbdillāh ibn Taymiyyah in their commentaries on the Qurʾān, and it is the view of Ibn Ḥazm al-Ẓāhirī. The first view is that of Mujāhid, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Thawrī and Aḥmad.
As for the marfūʿ hadith of Abū Hurayrah, “I do not know whether the prescribed punishments are a purification for those who receive them or not,”

al-Ḥākim and others recorded it, but al-Bukhārī found a defect in it and said: It is not established; it is only one of the mursal reports of al-Zuhrī, which are weak, and ʿAbd al-Razzāq erred in giving it a connected chain. He said: It is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that the prescribed punishments are an expiation.

Among the evidence cited by those who say that the prescribed punishment is not an expiation are the words of the Exalted about those who wage war: “That is a disgrace for them in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have a mighty punishment — except for those who repent before you overpower them” [al-Māʾidah 5:33–34]. Its apparent sense is that they receive both the punishment of this world and that of the Hereafter.

The reply is that He mentioned their punishment in this world and their punishment in the Hereafter, and it does not follow that the two are combined. As for the exception of “those who repent”, He made it from the punishment of this world only, for the punishment of the Hereafter is dropped by repentance whether before they are overpowered or after.
His words ﷺ, “And whoever commits any of these and Allah conceals it for him, his affair rests with Allah: if He wills, He punishes him,

and if He wills, He forgives him,” state explicitly that whoever meets Allah with these major sins is subject to His will. This shows that performing the obligations does not expiate or wipe them out,
for the generality of Muslims keep up the obligations, especially those from whom the Prophet ﷺ was taking the pledge.

Excluded from this is whoever meets Allah having repented of them, by the texts of the Book and the Sunnah showing that whoever repents to Allah, Allah accepts his repentance and forgives him. So whoever has not repented remains subject to the divine will.

Another indication that deeds do not expiate major sins is that Allah has not appointed any obligatory expiation in this world for major sins; He has appointed expiation only for minor ones, such as the expiation for intercourse by a man who has pronounced ẓihār,

for intercourse with a woman during menstruation according to the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās which Imam Aḥmad and others adopted, and for omitting one of the obligatory acts of Ḥajj or committing one of its prohibitions. These are of four kinds: a sacrificial animal,

freeing a slave, charity and fasting. That is why, according to the majority of scholars, no expiation is due for deliberate killing, nor, according to most of them, for the wilfully false oath (al-yamīn al-ghamūs). The killer is merely encouraged, as a recommendation, to free a slave,

as in the hadith of Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ: they came to the Prophet ﷺ about a companion of theirs who had made [the Fire] due for himself, and he said: “Free a slave on his behalf; by it Allah will free him from the Fire.”
“Made due” means he did a deed by which the Fire became due for him; it is said that he had killed someone.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: Ibn ʿUmar struck a slave of his and then freed him, and said: I have no reward in it, not even this much — and he picked up a twig from the ground. I heard the Prophet ﷺ say:
“Whoever slaps his slave or beats him, his expiation is to free him.”

If it is said: The man who has intercourse in Ramaḍān is commanded to make expiation, and breaking the fast in Ramaḍān is a major sin — the reply is: The expiation is not for breaking the fast. That is why, according to most scholars, it is not obligatory for everyone who deliberately breaks the fast in Ramaḍān;

it is only for violating the sanctity of a day of Ramaḍān by intercourse. That is why, if he had already broken his fast in a way not permitted to him during a day of Ramaḍān and then had intercourse, the expiation would be binding on him according to Imam Aḥmad, for the reason we have given.

Among the evidence that the expiating effect of obligatory deeds is restricted to minor sins is what al-Bukhārī recorded from Ḥudhayfah, who said: While we were sitting with ʿUmar, he said: Which of you remembers what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said about trial (fitnah)?

I said: “A man's trial in his family, his wealth, his children and his neighbour is expiated by prayer, charity, enjoining good and forbidding evil.” He said: It is not this that I am asking you about.

Muslim recorded something with the same meaning. The apparent sense of this wording is that it is marfūʿ, and in one narration of al-Bukhārī Ḥudhayfah said: I heard him say, “A man's trial…” and he mentioned it — which is all but explicit that it is marfūʿ. In one narration of Muslim's, it is the words of ʿUmar.

As for the Prophet's words ﷺ to the man who said to him, “I have committed an offence carrying a prescribed punishment, so carry it out on me,” whom he left until he had prayed and then told, “Allah has forgiven you your offence (ḥadd)” — this is not explicit that a major sin is meant,

because the ḥudūd of Allah are what He has forbidden, as the Exalted said: “Those are the limits (ḥudūd) of Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has wronged himself” [al-Ṭalāq 65:1]; and His words: “Those are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them” [al-Baqarah 2:229]; and His words:

“Those are the limits of Allah; whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to Gardens…” — the verse — up to His words: “And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding in it for ever, and he will have a humiliating punishment” [al-Nisāʾ 4:13–14].
In the hadith of al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, from the Prophet ﷺ, in which he likened Islam to the straight path with a wall on each side, he said: “The two walls are the limits of Allah.”
It has already been cited in full.
So whoever commits anything Allah has forbidden has encroached on His limits, violated them and transgressed them.

And supposing that the offence he committed was a major sin, this man came remorseful and repentant and gave himself up to have the punishment carried out on him; remorse is repentance, and repentance expiates major sins without any doubt. Something has also been narrated that is cited as evidence that major sins are expiated by certain righteous deeds.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, I have committed a terrible sin; is there any repentance for me?
He said: “Do you have a mother?”
He said: No. He said: “Do you have a maternal aunt?”

He said: Yes. He said: “Then be dutiful to her.” Ibn Ḥibbān recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ, as did al-Ḥākim, who said: It meets the conditions of al-Bukhārī and Muslim. But al-Tirmidhī recorded it by another route as mursal and stated that the mursal version is more authentic than the connected one, and ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and al-Dāraquṭnī said the same.
It has been narrated that a man said to ʿUmar: I have killed someone. He said: Is your mother alive?
He said: No. He said: And your father?

He said: Yes. He said: Then be dutiful to him and treat him well. Then ʿUmar said: If his mother were alive and he were dutiful to her and treated her well, I would hope that the Fire would never consume him.
Something with the same meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Likewise there is the woman who had practised sorcery at Dūmat al-Jandal: she came to Madīnah asking about her repentance, and found that the Prophet ﷺ had died. His Companions said to her: If your parents, or one of them, were alive, they would suffice you.
Al-Ḥākim recorded it and said: It contains the consensus of the Companions, soon after the death of the Messenger ﷺ, that dutifulness to parents would suffice her.
Makḥūl and Imam Aḥmad said: Dutifulness to parents is an expiation for major sins.
It has been narrated from some of the Salaf that carrying funeral biers removes major sins, and this has been narrated as marfūʿ by routes that are not authentic.
It is authentically reported, from the narration of Abū Burdah, that when death came to Abū Mūsā he said: My sons, remember the man of the loaf.

There was a man who worshipped in a hermitage for — I think — seventy years. Then Satan made a woman seem beautiful in his eyes, and he was with her for seven days and seven nights. Then the veil was lifted from the man,

and he went out repenting. Then he mentioned that he spent the night among some poor people, to whom a loaf each was given in charity. They gave him a loaf, and the one who used to be given it went without.

When he learned of that, he gave him the loaf, and by morning he was dead. The seventy years were weighed against the seven nights, and the nights outweighed them; then the loaf was weighed against the seven nights, and the loaf outweighed them.
Ibn al-Mubārak narrated, with his chain, in his book al-Birr wa-l-Ṣilah, that Ibn Masʿūd said: A man worshipped Allah for seventy years, then committed an indecency, and Allah nullified his deeds.

Then he was struck by a chronic illness and crippled. He saw a man giving charity to some poor people, so he went to him, took a loaf from him and gave it in charity to a poor man; and Allah forgave him and restored to him the deeds of seventy years.
None of these shows that major sins are expiated by deeds alone,

because everyone mentioned in them was remorseful and repentant of his sin. What they asked about was only a righteous deed by which to draw near to Allah after repentance, so as to wipe out the trace of the sin entirely.
For Allah has made righteous deeds a condition for the acceptance of repentance and the forgiveness of sins by it, as in His words:

“Except for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds” [Maryam 19:60], His words: “I am Most Forgiving towards whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds” [Ṭā Hā 20:82], and His words: “As for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, it may be that he will be among the successful” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:67].
This gives a foothold to those who say that the one who repents is still subject to the divine will after his repentance, and this was the state of many of the fearful among the Salaf.
One of them said to a man: Have you committed a sin?
He said: Yes. He said: Do you know that Allah has recorded it against you?
He said: Yes. He said: Then work until you know that Allah has wiped it out.

Of the same kind is the saying of Ibn Masʿūd: The believer sees his sins as though he were at the foot of a mountain that he fears will fall on him, while the wicked man sees his sins like a fly that has landed on his nose, and he does like this to it [waving it away]. Al-Bukhārī recorded it.
They used to suspect their deeds and their repentance, fearing that they had not been accepted from them, and this produced in them intense fear and great effort in righteous deeds.
Al-Ḥasan said: I met people who, had one of them spent the earth's fill, would still not have felt safe, so great did sin seem to him.

Ibn ʿAwn said: Do not trust in the abundance of your deeds, for you do not know whether they will be accepted from you or not; and do not feel safe about your sins, for you do not know whether they have been expiated for you or not. All your deeds are hidden from you.

The most evident view on this question — that is, the expiation of major sins by deeds — is, and Allah knows best, that if it is meant that major sins are wiped out merely by performing the obligations, and are expiated by that just as minor sins are expiated by avoiding major ones, then this is false.

But if it is meant that on the Day of Resurrection major sins may be weighed against certain deeds, so that the major sin is wiped out by the deed that balances it and the deed is dropped, leaving no reward for it, then this may happen.

We have already cited from Ibn ʿUmar that when he freed the slave he had struck, he said that he had no reward in it, since it was an expiation for his sin — and his sin was not a major one. What then of deeds that expiate major sins?

We have also cited the view of those of the Salaf who said that a bad deed is wiped out and a corresponding good deed, from among the good deeds that are the reward of the deed, is dropped. If that is so with minor sins, what then of major ones?
For some major sins may nullify certain deeds that conflict with them, as reproach and hurt nullify charity, and dealing in usury nullifies jihād, as ʿĀʾishah said.

Ḥudhayfah said: Falsely accusing a chaste woman demolishes the deeds of a hundred years — and it has also been narrated from him as marfūʿ, recorded by al-Bazzār. And just as abandoning the ʿAṣr prayer nullifies deeds, it is not to be thought strange that the reward of the deed that expiates major sins should be nullified.

Al-Bazzār in his Musnad and al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “A servant's good deeds and bad deeds will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and some will be offset — or settled — against others. If one good deed remains to him, his place in Paradise will be widened by it.”
Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Lahīʿah, who said: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dīnār told me, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, about the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:
“Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it” [al-Zalzalah 99:7]. He said: The Muslims used to think they would not be rewarded for something small if they gave it.

A poor man would come, and they would think it too little to give him a date, a piece of bread, a walnut or the like, and would turn him away, saying: This is nothing; we are rewarded only for giving what we love. Others thought they would not be blamed for a small sin, such as a lie, a glance, backbiting and the like, saying:
Allah has threatened the Fire only for major sins. So Allah encouraged them to do small acts of good, for they may soon become many,

and warned them against small evils, for they may soon become many. So this was revealed: “Whoever does an atom's weight” — meaning the weight of the smallest ant — “of good will see it” — meaning in his record —
and it will please him. He said: For every righteous and wicked person, each bad deed is recorded as one bad deed and each good deed as ten good deeds. Then on the Day of Resurrection

Allah will multiply the believer's good deeds again, each one by ten, and wipe out for him ten bad deeds for every good deed; and whoever's good deeds exceed his bad deeds by an atom's weight will enter Paradise.

The apparent sense of this is that good and bad deeds are offset against each other, then the good deeds set against the bad ones are dropped, and what is left over after the offsetting is considered. This agrees with the view of those who say that whoever's good deeds outweigh his bad deeds by one good deed is rewarded for that good deed alone,

while the rest of his good deeds are dropped against his bad deeds — contrary to those who say that he is rewarded for all of them and his bad deeds are dropped as though they had never been. This concerns major sins. As for minor sins,
they may be wiped out by righteous deeds while the reward of those deeds remains, as he ﷺ said: “Shall I not direct you to that by which Allah wipes out wrongs

and raises degrees? Performing wuḍūʾ thoroughly in difficult conditions, taking many steps to the mosques, and waiting for one prayer after another.” So he affirmed that these deeds both expiate wrongs and raise degrees. Likewise his words ﷺ: “Whoever says, ‘There is no god but Allah alone, without partner;

His is the dominion and His is the praise; He gives life and causes death, and He has power over all things,’ a hundred times, Allah writes for him a hundred good deeds, a hundred bad deeds are wiped out from him, and it is equal for him to freeing ten slaves.” This shows that remembrance wipes out bad deeds while its reward remains, multiplied, for the one who does it.
Likewise the bad deeds of one who repents sincerely are expiated for him while his good deeds remain for him, as Allah the Exalted said:

“Until, when he reaches his full strength and reaches forty years, he says: My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed on me and on my parents, and to do righteous deeds that please You, and make my offspring righteous for me. I have repented to You, and I am among the Muslims. Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they did and whose bad deeds We pass over, among the companions of Paradise — the true promise which they were promised” [al-Aḥqāf 46:15–16].

And the Exalted said: “And the one who brought the truth and those who confirmed it — it is they who are the God-fearing. They will have whatever they wish with their Lord; that is the reward of those who do good, so that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them according to the best of what they used to do” [al-Zumar 39:33–35].
Since He described these people with taqwā and excellence, this shows that they do not persist in sins but repent of them.
His words, “so that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did”, include major sins,

because they are the worst of deeds. And He said: “Whoever fears Allah, He will remove his bad deeds from him and make his reward great” [al-Ṭalāq 65:5], making the removal of bad deeds and the magnifying of reward follow from taqwā, which includes doing obligations and leaving what is forbidden. And Allah told of the believers who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth that they said:

“Our Lord, we have heard a caller calling to faith: ‘Believe in your Lord,’ and we have believed. Our Lord, so forgive us our sins, remove from us our bad deeds, and take us in death with the righteous” [Āl ʿImrān 3:193]. He told us that He answered this prayer for them, removed their bad deeds from them and admitted them to the Gardens.
In His words, “forgive us our sins, remove from us our bad deeds”, Allah assigned forgiveness to sins and removal to bad deeds.
So it may be said: “Bad deeds” are specifically minor sins, while “sins” means major sins. Bad deeds are removed by expiation,

because Allah has appointed expiations for them in this world, both in the Sharīʿah and by decree, whereas sins need a forgiveness that protects the sinner from their evil. Forgiveness and expiation are close in meaning: forgiveness (maghfirah) has been said to be the covering of sins, and also to be protection from the evil of the sin together with covering it.

That is why what covers and protects the head in war is called a mighfar [helmet], while not everything that covers the head is called a mighfar. Allah has told us that the angels pray for the repentant believers to be forgiven and protected from bad deeds. Expiation (takfīr) is of the same kind,
because the root meaning of kufr too is covering and concealing.

Some later scholars distinguished between them by saying that expiation is wiping out the trace of the sin as though it had never been, while forgiveness includes, besides that, Allah's bounty and generosity to the servant. This is questionable.

It may also be explained by saying that forgiveness of sins through righteous deeds turns them into good deeds, while expiating them through things that expiate merely wipes them out. This too is questionable, for it is authentically reported that sins punished by entering the Fire are changed into good deeds; so sins expiated by a righteous deed that serves as their expiation are all the more so.
It may bear two further meanings.
One is that forgiveness occurs only where there is no punishment and no taking to account,

because it is protection from the evil of the sin altogether, whereas expiation may come after punishment: all worldly calamities expiate wrongs, and they are punishments. Likewise pardon comes both with punishment and without it, and so does mercy.
