The second is that expiations are those deeds that Allah has appointed for wiping out the sins they expiate, and that is their reward; they have no reward besides it.
For the most part they are of the kind that goes against the soul's inclinations and involves bearing hardship, like avoiding major sins, which Allah has made an expiation for minor ones.
The deeds by which sins are forgiven are all the rest, and in them forgiveness and reward for the deed come together, as with remembrance, by which good deeds are written and bad deeds wiped out.

On this view a distinction is made between deeds that are expiations and other deeds. As for the expiation and forgiveness of sins when attributed to Allah, there is no difference between them — though on the first view there is a difference between them here too.
Two things bear out this second view.
The first is what Ibn ʿUmar said when he freed the slave he had struck: I have no reward in freeing him — and he gave as his reason that it was an expiation.

The second is that all worldly calamities expiate sins, and many of the Companions and others of the Salaf said that there is no reward in them besides the expiation, though some of them disagreed on this.

It should not be objected: “In the hadith of the dream the expiations were explained as performing wuḍūʾ thoroughly in hateful conditions and walking to the prayers, and he said: Whoever does that lives well and dies well, and is as free of his wrongs as on the day his mother bore him.

All of these, besides expiating bad deeds, raise degrees and earn reward.” For we say: two things may come together in a single deed, one of which raises degrees while the other expiates bad deeds. Wuḍūʾ itself is rewarded,
but performing it thoroughly in severe cold belongs to the kind of pain that souls suffer in this world, so in that situation it is an expiation; in other situations wrongs are forgiven by it

as they are forgiven by remembrance and other deeds. Likewise walking to the congregational prayers is an act of devotion and obedience for which one is rewarded, but the hardship and pain the soul suffers in it through fatigue and toil is an expiation.

Likewise, keeping oneself in the mosque to wait for the prayer, and cutting the soul off from its habit of going out to places it inclines to, whether to earn worldly gain or for recreation, is painful to the soul in this respect, and so it is an expiation.
It has come in the hadith that one of the two steps of a person walking to the mosque raises him a degree and the other removes a wrong from him.
This strengthens what we have said: that what brings about expiation is other than what brings about the raising of degrees. And Allah knows best.
On this basis, the expiation of bad deeds and the raising of degrees come together in a single deed from two different aspects, and in every case it may be described in both ways.
There is no contradiction, then, between calling it an expiation and saying that its reward is multiplied, or describing it as raising degrees. That is why he ﷺ said:

“The five prayers, from one Friday to the next, and from one Ramaḍān to the next, are expiations for what is between them, as long as major sins are avoided.” For in holding the soul to keeping up the obligations there is something that goes against its inclinations and restrains it from what it inclines to, and that brings about the expiation of minor sins.
Likewise martyrdom in the path of Allah expiates sins through the pain it involves, and raises degrees through the righteous deeds of heart and body that accompany it.
It is clear from this that some deeds combine, from two aspects, what brings about the raising of degrees and the expiation of bad deeds, with no contradiction between them.

This is established without doubt for minor sins. As for major sins, they may be expiated by martyrdom while the martyr still receives his reward; but the martyr who carries sins is in the fourth of the ranks of martyrs,
as has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Faḍālah ibn ʿUbayd, recorded by Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī.

As for the forgiveness of sins by certain deeds while their wage and reward are kept in full, the authentic hadiths on remembrance indicate it. It has also been said that those bad deeds are written as good deeds too,

as in the hadith of Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī cited earlier. We also mentioned from one of the Salaf that against a single bad deed one multiple of a good deed's reward is wiped out, and nine good deeds remain for him.

The apparent sense is that this is specific to minor sins. In the Hereafter, however, good and bad deeds are weighed against each other and some are offset against others, and whoever's good deeds outweigh his bad deeds is saved

and enters Paradise; and in this minor and major sins are alike. So too whoever has good deeds to his credit but owes wrongs to others: if those he wronged take their rights in full from his good deeds and one good deed remains to him, he enters Paradise by it.
Ibn Masʿūd said: If he is a friend of Allah and an atom's weight is left over for him, Allah multiplies it for him until he enters Paradise; but if he is wretched, the angel says:
My Lord, his good deeds are used up, and many claimants against him remain. He says: Take from their bad deeds and add them to his, then write him a warrant to the Fire.
Ibn Abī Ḥātim and others recorded it.

What is meant is that an atom's weight of good deeds being left over comes only from the bounty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through His multiplying of the believer's good deeds and blessing in them. So it is with whoever has good and bad deeds

and Allah wills to show him mercy: enough of his good deeds is left over to admit him into Paradise, and all of it is from Allah's bounty and mercy, for no one enters Paradise except by Allah's bounty and mercy.

Abū Nuʿaym recorded with a weak chain, from ʿAlī as marfūʿ: “Allah revealed to one of the prophets of the Children of Israel: Say to the people of obedience to Me among your community: Let them not rely on their deeds, for there is no servant whom I call strictly to account on the Day of Resurrection, wishing to punish him, but I punish him.

And say to the people of disobedience to Me among your community: Let them not cast themselves into ruin, for I forgive the gravest sin and do not mind.” This is confirmed by the Prophet's words ﷺ in the authentic hadith: “Whoever is scrutinised in the reckoning is punished,” and in one narration: “is ruined.” And Allah knows best.
The second question: is repentance from minor sins obligatory, as it is from major sins, or not,

since they are expiated by avoiding major sins, according to the words of the Exalted: “If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove your bad deeds from you and admit you by a noble entrance” [al-Nisāʾ 4:31]?
This is a matter on which people have differed.
Some held that repentance from them is obligatory. This is the view of the scholars of our school and of others among the jurists, the theologians and others.
Allah commanded repentance right after mentioning minor and major sins, saying:

“Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them; Allah is aware of what they do. And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts…” up to His words: “Repent to Allah all together, O believers, that you may succeed” [al-Nūr 24:30–31].
And He commanded repentance from minor sins specifically, in the words of the Exalted:

“O you who believe, let no people mock another people; perhaps they are better than them. Nor let women mock other women; perhaps they are better than them. Do not find fault with one another or call one another by offensive nicknames. How evil is the name of wickedness after faith! And whoever does not repent — it is they who are the wrongdoers” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:11].

Some did not hold repentance from them to be obligatory; this is reported from a group of the Muʿtazilah. Some later scholars said that one of two things is obligatory: either repenting of them, or doing some of the good deeds that expiate sins.
Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reported in his Tafsīr two views on the expiation of minor sins by carrying out the obligations and avoiding the major sins.

The first — which he reported from a number of jurists and hadith scholars — is that one can be absolutely certain they are expiated by that, because of the apparent sense of the verse and the hadith.
The second — which he reported from the legal theorists — is that one cannot be certain of it; rather, it is to be taken as a strong probability and a strong hope,

and it is subject to the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For if their expiation were certain, minor sins would have the status of what is permissible and carries no consequences, and that would undo the bonds of the Sharīʿah.
I say: It may be said that their expiation is not certain,

because the hadiths that mention expiation by deeds without qualification have come elsewhere qualified by doing the deed well, as with wuḍūʾ and prayer, and so one cannot be sure that the good performance which brings about expiation is present. The disagreement over whether repentance from minor sins is obligatory rests on this disagreement that Ibn ʿAṭiyyah mentioned.

Ibn Jarīr recorded, from the narration of al-Ḥasan, that some people came to ʿUmar and said: We see things in the Book of Allah that are not acted upon. He said to one of them: Have you read the whole Qurʾān?
He said: Yes. He said: Have you fulfilled all of it in yourself?
He said: By Allah, no. He said: Have you fulfilled all of it in your sight?
Have you fulfilled all of it in your speech?
Have you fulfilled all of it in your actions?
Then he went through them one by one until he came to the last of them, and said: May ʿUmar's mother lose him! Do you want to burden him with making people keep the Book of Allah?
Our Lord knew that we would have bad deeds. And he recited: “If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove your bad deeds from you and admit you by a noble entrance” [al-Nisāʾ 4:31].

And with his chain, from Anas ibn Mālik, that he said: I have never seen anything like what has reached us from our Lord the Exalted — and yet we have not left every family and possession for its sake! Then he fell silent, and then said:

By Allah, our Lord has charged us with less than that: He has passed over for us whatever is short of the major sins, so what have we to do with them? Then he recited: “If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove your bad deeds from you and admit you by a noble entrance” [al-Nisāʾ 4:31].
Al-Bazzār recorded it in his Musnad as marfūʿ, but the mawqūf version is more authentic.

Allah has described those who do good as avoiding major sins. The Exalted said: “And that He may reward those who do good with the best: those who avoid the major sins and indecencies, except for lesser faults (lamam). Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness” [al-Najm 53:31–32].
The Salaf held two views on the explanation of lamam.

One is that it is the preliminaries of indecencies, such as touching and kissing. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It is whatever falls short of the [two] limits: the threat of the Fire in the Hereafter and the prescribed punishment in this world.

The second is that it is falling into one of the indecencies or major sins once and then repenting of it. This has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah, and from Abū Hurayrah as marfūʿ, with doubt as to whether it is marfūʿ.

He said: It is a single lapse into fornication, after which he repents and does not go back to it; a single lapse into drinking wine, after which he repents and does not go back to it; a single lapse into theft, after which he repents and does not go back to it.
Those who explain the verse in this way say that he must repent of it, unlike those who explain it as the preliminaries, who do not make repentance a condition.
What seems correct is that both views are sound and that both are meant by the verse. In that case, the one who does good is the one who commits a major sin only rarely and then repents of it,

and who, when he commits a minor sin, has it submerged in his good deeds that expiate it — provided he does not persist in it, as the Exalted said: “and do not persist knowingly in what they have done” [Āl ʿImrān 3:135].
It has been narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said: No sin is minor when one persists in it, and no sin is major when one asks forgiveness for it. This has also been narrated as marfūʿ by weak routes.

Since minor sins become major by being persisted in, those who do good must avoid persisting in minor sins, so that they may be among those who avoid major sins and indecencies. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“What is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely on their Lord; who avoid the major sins and indecencies, and when they are angry, they forgive; who respond to their Lord, establish the prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation and spend from what We have provided for them; and who, when wronged, defend themselves. The recompense for a bad deed is a bad deed like it; but whoever pardons and makes peace, his reward rests with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers” [al-Shūrā 42:36–40].

These verses describe the believers as fulfilling what Allah has made obligatory for them — faith, reliance on Allah, establishing the prayer, spending from what Allah has provided for them, and responding to Allah in all acts of obedience to Him —

while at the same time avoiding major sins and indecencies; and that is the realisation of taqwā. In their dealings with people He describes them as forgiving when angry, and He encourages them to pardon and make peace.
As for His words:

“and who, when wronged, defend themselves” [al-Shūrā 42:39], this does not conflict with pardon, for defending oneself consists in showing one's ability to take revenge, and the pardon then comes after that, which makes it more complete and perfect.
Al-Nakhaʿī said about this verse: They disliked being humiliated, but when they had the power, they pardoned.

Mujāhid said: They disliked that a believer should humiliate himself and so embolden the wicked against him. So when the believer is wronged, he shows his ability to take revenge, and then pardons. Something like this happened to many of the Salaf, among them Qatādah and others.
These verses contain everything the Prophet ﷺ mentioned in his counsel to Muʿādh. They contain the foundations of the traits of taqwā: doing what is obligatory,

refraining from the gravest of forbidden things, and dealing with people through kindness and pardon. It follows from this that if they commit some sin other than the major sins and indecencies, it is submerged in the traits of taqwā, which bring about its expiation and erasure.

As for the verses in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, in them He described the God-fearing as doing good to people, asking forgiveness for indecencies and for wronging themselves, and not persisting in that. This is the most complete state: to make a fresh repentance
and ask forgiveness after every sin, whether small or great, as it has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ counselled Muʿādh to do, which we mentioned earlier.
We have dealt with this at length only
because people's need of it is great: everyone needs to know this and then to act on it. Allah is the One who grants success and help.

His words ﷺ, “Follow a bad deed with a good one and it will wipe it out”, plainly indicate that bad deeds are wiped out by good deeds. We have already cited the reports stating that a bad deed is wiped out from the angels' scrolls by a good deed done after it.
ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī said: I have been told that whoever weeps over a wrong has it wiped out from him, and a good deed is written for him.

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr said: Whoever remembers a wrong he has done, and his heart trembles at it, and he asks forgiveness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, nothing holds it back until the Most Merciful wipes it out from him.
Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith said: I was told that al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: Weeping by day wipes out public sins, and weeping by night wipes out secret sins.
We have cited the words of the Prophet ﷺ: “Shall I not direct you to that by which Allah wipes out wrongs and raises degrees?” — the hadith.

A group said: Sins are not wiped out from the scrolls of deeds by repentance or anything else; rather, their doer must be made to stand before them and read them on the Day of Resurrection. They cited the words of the Exalted:

“The record will be laid down, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, saying: Woe to us! What is this record that leaves nothing small or great unaccounted for?” [al-Kahf 18:49]. Using this verse as evidence is questionable,

because it mentions only the state of the criminals, the people of crimes and grave sins, and the believers who have repented of their sins, or whose sins are submerged in their good deeds, are not included among them.
A clearer argument is from His words: “Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it” [al-Zalzalah 99:7–8].
Some exegetes have stated that this is the correct view among the most careful scholars. It has been narrated from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Bilāl ibn Saʿd al-Dimashqī.
Al-Ḥasan said about the servant who sins and then repents and asks forgiveness: He is forgiven, but it is not wiped out from his record without His making him stand before it
and then asking him about it. Then al-Ḥasan wept bitterly and said: Even if we wept only out of shame at that standing, it would be right for us to weep.
Bilāl ibn Saʿd said: Allah forgives sins, but He does not wipe them out from the scroll until He has made the servant stand before them on the Day of Resurrection, even if he has repented.
Abū Hurayrah said: On the Day of Resurrection Allah will bring the servant near, place His covering over him and screen him from all creatures, and hand him his record within that screen.
He will say: Read your record, son of Ādam. He reads, and comes to a good deed, and his face shines white because of it and his heart rejoices at it. Allah says: Do you recognise it, My servant?

He says: Yes. He says: I have accepted it from you. He prostrates, and He says: Raise your head and go back to your record. He comes to a bad deed, and his face darkens because of it, his heart trembles at it, his flesh quivers at it, and such shame before his Lord takes hold of him as no one else knows. He says: Do you recognise it, My servant?
He says: Yes, my Lord. He says: I have forgiven it for you. He prostrates, and all that the creatures see of him is his prostrating, until they call out to one another:
Glad tidings for this servant, who never disobeyed Allah! They do not know what he has been through, between himself and his Lord, in what He made him stand before.

Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī said, from Salmān: On the Day of Resurrection a man will be given his scroll. He reads the top of it, and there are his bad deeds; and when he is about to lose hope, he looks at the bottom of it, and there are his good deeds. Then he looks at the top again, and they have been changed into good deeds.
It has also been narrated from Abū ʿUthmān, from Ibn Masʿūd, and from Abū ʿUthmān as his own words, which is more authentic.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated, with his chain, from one of the companions of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, who said: The people of Paradise will enter Paradise in four classes: the God-fearing, then the grateful, then the fearful, then the companions of the right.
He was asked: Why are they called the companions of the right?

He said: Because they did both good and bad deeds and were given their records in their right hands. They read their bad deeds letter by letter and said: Our Lord, these are our bad deeds; where are our good deeds?
Then Allah wiped out the bad deeds and made them good deeds, and at that they said: “Here, read my record!” [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19]. They are the majority of the people of Paradise.

Those who hold this view may take the hadiths on bad deeds being wiped out by good deeds to mean the wiping out of their punishment, not the wiping out of their record from the scrolls. And Allah knows best.
His words ﷺ, “and treat people with good character”: this is one of the traits of taqwā, and taqwā is not complete without it. He mentioned it separately only because it needed to be made clear,

for many people think that taqwā is fulfilling the rights of Allah and not the rights of His servants. So he expressly commanded him to treat people well. He had sent him to Yemen as their teacher, their instructor in the religion and their judge, and someone in that position

needs to treat people with good character more than others do who are not needed by people and do not mix with them. It often happens that those who devote themselves to fulfilling the rights of Allah

and give themselves over to His love, fear and obedience neglect the rights of His servants entirely or fall short in them. Combining the fulfilment of Allah's rights with the rights of His servants is very rare; only the most perfect of the prophets and the truthful (ṣiddīqūn) are equal to it.
Al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī said: Three things are rare or non-existent: a beautiful face with chastity, good character with religious devotion, and good brotherhood with trustworthiness.
One of the Salaf said: Dāwūd (peace be upon him) sat alone, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: Why do I see you alone?
He said: I have forsaken people for Your sake, Lord of the worlds. He said: Dāwūd, shall I not direct you to that by which you will keep people's goodwill and attain My pleasure?
Treat people according to their characters, and keep faith secure between Me and you.

Allah has counted treating people with good character among the traits of taqwā in His Book; indeed, He began with it, in His words: “prepared for the God-fearing, who spend in ease and in hardship, who restrain their rage and pardon people — and Allah loves those who do good” [Āl ʿImrān 3:133–134].

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated, with his chain, that Saʿīd al-Maqburī said: We have been told that a man came to ʿĪsā son of Maryam (peace be upon him) and said: Teacher of good, how can I be God-fearing towards Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He deserves?

He said: By a simple matter: love Allah with all your heart, work with your toil and strength as much as you can, and show mercy to your fellow kind as you show mercy to yourself. He said: Who are my fellow kind, teacher of good?
He said: All the children of Ādam. And what you would not like to be done to you, do not do to anyone; then you will be God-fearing towards Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He deserves.

The Prophet ﷺ made good character one of the finest traits of faith, as Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The most complete of the believers in faith are those best in character.”
Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī recorded it with the addition: “A man may be a believer and yet have something in his character that diminishes his faith.”
Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Usāmah ibn Sharīk, that he said: They said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the best thing a Muslim has been given?
He said: “Good character.”

The Prophet ﷺ told us that a person of good character reaches by his character the rank of one who fasts and prays at night, so that whoever seeks taqwā should not be distracted from good character by fasting and prayer,

thinking that good character will cut him off from their merit. Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “By his good character the believer attains the ranks of one who fasts and stands in prayer at night.”

He also told us that good character is the heaviest thing placed in the Balance, and that its possessor is the dearest of people to Allah and the closest of them in seating to the prophets. Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ,
that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Nothing placed in the Balance is heavier than good character, and the person of good character attains by it the rank of the person of fasting and prayer.”

Ibn Ḥibbān recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Shall I not tell you who is dearest of you to Allah and closest of you to me in seating on the Day of Resurrection?”
They said: Yes indeed. He said:
“Those of you who are best in character.” The hadith of Abū Hurayrah has already been cited, from the Prophet ﷺ: “What most often admits people into Paradise is fear of Allah and good character.”

Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “I guarantee a house in the highest part of Paradise for whoever makes his character good.” Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Anas.
Explanations of good character have been narrated from the Salaf. Al-Ḥasan said: Good character is generosity, open-handedness and forbearance.
Al-Shaʿbī said: Good character is open-handedness, giving and a warm, cheerful face; and al-Shaʿbī was like that.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: It is a cheerful face, generous kindness and refraining from harm.
Sallām ibn Abī Muṭīʿ was asked about good character, and he recited:
You see him, when you come to him, beaming with joy, / as though you were giving him what you have come to ask of him.
Were there nothing in his hand but his own soul, / he would give it away — so let whoever asks of him fear Allah.
He is the sea: from whichever side you approach it, / its depths are kindness and generosity is its shore.
Imam Aḥmad said: Good character is that you do not become angry or lose your temper. It is also narrated that he said: Good character is that you bear whatever comes from people.
Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said: It is a cheerful face and not becoming angry; and Muḥammad ibn Naṣr said something similar.
One of the people of knowledge said: Good character is restraining one's rage for Allah's sake; showing cheerfulness and a smiling face, except to the innovator and the wicked;

pardoning those who slip, except to discipline them or carry out a prescribed punishment; and keeping harm from every Muslim and every person under covenant, except to change a wrong or to take back what is owed to someone wronged, without transgressing.

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Anas al-Juhanī, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The most excellent of virtues is that you keep ties with whoever cuts you off, give to whoever withholds from you, and overlook it when someone reviles you.”
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir al-Juhanī, that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me:
“ʿUqbah, shall I not tell you the most excellent character of the people of this world and the Hereafter?
That you keep ties with whoever cuts you off, give to whoever withholds from you, and pardon whoever wrongs you.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of ʿAlī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Shall I not direct you to the noblest character of the people of this world and the Hereafter?
That you keep ties with whoever cuts you off, give to whoever withholds from you, and pardon whoever wrongs you.”
